# Quality gates catch repeatable mistakes {#sec-quality}

Tools are useful when they run before review and give the same result locally and in CI. Make
the safe path the short command.

## Warnings belong to the code that owns them {#sec-warnings}

Treat warnings as errors for first-party targets. Keep third-party headers as system headers
instead of muting your own warnings. Qt strict mode turns risky compatibility APIs into
compile errors before they become bugs.

Set warning options on your own targets, so they do not become requirements for every consumer
or third-party dependency. `cmake/AppTargetDefaults.cmake` applies the template's settings to
first-party targets.

## Qt strict mode {#sec-strict-mode}

`QT_ENABLE_STRICT_MODE_UP_TO` disables selected APIs that Qt considers error-prone up to the
version you specify. The template also enables `QT_NO_CAST_FROM_ASCII`: a byte string must be
converted to a `QString` deliberately. For example, use `QString::fromUtf8()` when UTF-8 data
comes from outside the program, or a Qt string literal when the text is known at compile time.
Explicit conversion makes the encoding part of the code rather than a guess.

## Sanitizers find memory mistakes early {#sec-sanitizers}

Run an AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer build regularly. They cost more than a
normal test run but turn memory corruption into a stack trace near the cause.

AddressSanitizer detects problems such as use-after-free and buffer overflows;
UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer detects several kinds of undefined behaviour. ThreadSanitizer
looks for data races, but needs a separate build from AddressSanitizer.

```sh
cmake --workflow --preset asan
```

## Hardening stays in the release {#sec-hardening}

Sanitizers are diagnostic builds. Compiler and standard-library hardening adds selected
checks to release builds too. It can make some memory errors fail closer to their cause; it
does not replace tests or sanitizers. The template configures its first-party targets in
`cmake/AppTargetDefaults.cmake`.

## One check answers one question {#sec-linters}

```sh
cmake --build --preset dev --target check
cmake --build --preset dev --target format
```

The check target combines C++ formatting and analysis, QML checks, and REUSE when their tools
are available. The format target changes formatting in place, so review its result before
staging.

The build helper checks which optional tools are available and may skip a check if its tool is
missing. Read the output rather than assuming that a successful target ran every optional tool.

## QML tooling keeps the view typed {#sec-qml-tools}

Use `qmllint` to catch QML type, binding, and import problems. Use `qmlformat` for
consistent layout. Use `qmlls` in an editor for the same feedback while writing. The module
metadata generated by `qt_add_qml_module()` makes those tools useful.

::: {.more}
**Template:** `cmake/Checks.cmake`, `.qmllint.ini`, and `.qmlformat.ini`

**Read more:** [QML tooling](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qtqml-tooling.html).
:::
